claim_verdicts.evidence: 11.6: "PostgreSQL automatically creates a unique index when a unique constraint or primary key is defined for a table. ... and is the mechanism that enforces the constraint." 5.5.3: "Unique constraints ensure that the data contained in a column, or a group of columns, is unique among all the rows in the table." The gloss 'no two rows share a value' ignores NULLs (not equal by default); harmless here, customers.email is NOT NULL.

5.5.5: "...the declaration of a foreign key constraint does not automatically create an index on the referencing columns." 11.1: "This adds overhead to data manipulation operations. Indexes can also prevent the creation of heap-only tuples." But 5.5.5 also: "a DELETE of a row from the referenced table or an UPDATE of a referenced column will require a scan of the referencing table", so an FK index can pay back with no app query; and 'each write' overstates (HOT updates).
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: Indexing them is left to you, because not every foreign key needs one: every index adds work to writes on its table, which an index that is rarely searched may not pay back.

claim_verdicts.evidence: Docs: "The view pg_indexes provides access to useful information about each index in the database." Tutorial 3.2: a view gives "a name to the query that you can refer to like an ordinary table." Live (donhang, read-only, 2026-09-28): pg_class.relkind for pg_indexes = 'v'; Try-it query returns 2 rows: order_items_pkey UNIQUE btree (order_id, product_id), payments_pkey UNIQUE btree (id). Round 1 scratch idxb_fk (stage-1 schema) gave the same.

"With no advance preparation, the system would have to scan the entire test1 table, row by row, to find all matching entries. ... But if the system has been instructed to maintain an index on the id column, it can use a more efficient method for locating matching rows."

11.3: "A multicolumn B-tree index can be used with query conditions that involve any subset of the index's columns, but the index is most efficient when there are constraints on the leading (leftmost) columns. The exact rule is that equality constraints on leading columns ... will be used to limit the portion of the index that is scanned." Lesson's 'later columns do not count the same way' is consistent (not 'cannot be used').

issues.text: Claim 2 rephrased. 'each write' overstates: PostgreSQL docs only say indexes add overhead to data manipulation and can prevent HOT updates. 'no query searches by never pays back' ignores 5.5.5: a DELETE of a parent row or UPDATE of a referenced column scans the referencing table, so an FK index can pay back with no application query.
issues.quote: every index adds work to each write, which a foreign key no query searches by never pays back
